title: Lab Journal — TensorRT, Triton and Custom Kernel Integration (scheduling & KV cache)
content:
Purpose and framing:
This is a lab-journal style writeup capturing experimental attempts to integrate TensorRT (TRT), Triton, and a small set of custom fused kernels into the serving runtime. Focus is on scheduler-kernel binding heuristics, KV cache interaction under streaming decode, and safe fallback mechanics when a preferred kernel is unavailable. Goal: pragmatic, reproducible notes (not a polished design doc).

Background and motivation:
- Customers want low p95 latency and predictability on common generation workloads while we keep unit-costs down. TRT gives good single-request latency for large models but has brittle cold-start and memory footprint behavior. Triton affords quick model switching and multitenant isolation but can incur overheads per-request. Custom fused kernels can improve token-throughput for narrow distributions but complicate scheduling and KV cache affinity.

High-level hypothesis we tested:
1) Optimistic binding: try high-performance kernel path (TRT/custom) for incoming requests; if it stalls on resource/memory, fall back to Triton-managed CPU/GPU path with minimal client-visible latency impact.
2) KV shadowing: maintain a light-weight shadow of KV cache state for fallback kernels so fallback does not require full KV reconstruction.
3) Hysteresis batching: scheduler should avoid flip-flopping between kernels on short timescales by adding confidence windows to kernel selection.

Experiment matrix (runs):
- Models: LLaMA-2-13B (HF->TRT export), Falcon-7B-instruct, small encoder-decoder pair used for reranking microbenchmarks.
- Kernels: TRT FP16 static (baseline high perf), Triton dynamic backend (baseline stable), custom_fuse_v1 (operator-fused attention+ffn for streaming), custom_async_io (I/O-optimized kernel that prefetches KV slices).
- Workloads: short-chat (avg tokens/request 40), long-chat (avg tokens/request 512), bursty-batch (100 concurrent short requests arriving in bursts).
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side), tokens/sec, GPU mem usage (resident), kernel switch events, fallback count, cold-start time (first request), and observed quality deviation (perplexity delta on held prompt set).

Key findings (summary):
1) Latency and cold-start tradeoffs:
   - TRT FP16 gave lowest p50 on single-request short-chat (p50 ~ 42ms), but cold-start for an idle TRT context could add 300-700ms on first request if kernels not resident.
   - Triton dynamic backend p50 ~ 55–70ms but cold-start hit was lower (80–150ms) because Triton amortizes model load across worker processes with lightweight loading.
   - Custom_fuse_v1 required 1.2x memory during warmup (temp tensors for fusion) which increased eviction pressure on KV cache for long-chat; as a result p95 regressed for sequences >256 tokens when fusion was enabled.

2) KV shadowing effectiveness:
   - We implemented a lightweight shadow that stores 1) per-request KV digest (hash + recent token index), 2) a compacted top-K recent KV slices (float16) keyed by request id.
   - On fallback from TRT->Triton, shadow allowed resuming decode with <60ms penalty vs full KV recompute (measured on 512-token stream) in 80% of cases.
   - Memory overhead of shadowing was ~8–12% for long-lived sessions; acceptable for Dedicated capacity but needs configurable caps for multitenant hosted API.

3) Scheduling hysteresis and flip-flop avoidance:
   - Naive per-request kernel selection caused oscillation: bursty workloads would cause scheduler to repeatedly swap kernels and thrash caches.
   - Introducing a 200–800ms confidence window (hysteresis) reduced kernel switch events by ~78% and improved p95 by ~18% in bursty-batch tests.

4) Fallback modes and graceful degradation:
   - Two-level fallback (fast path -> warm standby -> cold fallback) worked best. Warm standby is Triton worker with preloaded model but without TRT bindings; cold fallback is CPU-only path.
   - Warm standby requires KV shadow to minimize recompute cost; without shadow, warm standby cold start penalty made fallback worse than waiting for TRT to recover.

5) Quality/quantization interactions:
   - Mixed-precision (FP16) on TRT introduced small but measurable edge cases on very long prefix-conditioned generations (rare hallucination spikes on a 1-in-1000 prompt set). We flagged this for eval team to include in regression suites.

Implementation details (what we built quickly):
- KernelProbe harness: small in-runtime harness that can attach to a running worker and exercise a candidate kernel with a synthetic request to measure warmup time, memory delta, and throughput. Useful for online decisions.
- KV Shadow store: ring-buffer per-session with compacted float16 slices + rolling digest. API: compact_kv(session_id) -> digest; restore_kv(session_id, digest) -> best-effort restore.
- Scheduler heuristic implemented in a prototype as a middleware in the request path: it consults recent-session affinity, kernel health metrics (tracked live), and hysteresis window. It emits a trace span for each decision.

Reproduce (quick runbook):
- Checkout rt-runtime branch: feature/lab-trt-fallback
- Start local orchestrator (dev): docker-compose -f dev-compose.yml up --build (sets Triton and mock TRT service)
- Load model: ./scripts/register_model.sh --model llm-13b --backend triton --variant dynamic
- Run benchmark: python tools/bench_client.py --profile short-chat --concurrency 16 --duration 120
- Enable custom kernel: curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/admin/enable-kernel -d '{"name":"custom_fuse_v1"}' (dev only)
- Check kernel events: curl http://localhost:8080/admin/kernel-events | jq '.'

Observations and nuanced tradeoffs (notes to self):
- TRT is best for hot, pinned capacity where model residency can be guaranteed (Dedicated pools). For hosted API, warm-standby + shadowing is necessary to get TRT-like p50 without exposing cold-starts to customers.
- Custom fused kernels improve throughput for narrow distributions but are brittle to sequence-length variation and KV eviction patterns. They should be opt-in per-route with automatic guard-rails.
- Memory ambidexterity: we need tooling that can simulate kernel memory transient peaks (fusion temp tensors, TRT workspace) vs steady-state KV footprint. Current mem profiler misses short-lived 10s-100s ms spikes.

Open questions and experiments to run next:
1) Can we reduce TRT cold-start by snapshotting a hot-resident CUDAMemory image and restoring faster than reinitializing kernels? Prototype: 'thin-loader' that maps pre-initialized memory pages.
2) Can KV shadowing be tiered (hot recent slices in-memory, cold compact digest on disk) to support hosted scale without linear memory growth?
3) How to drive scheduler decisions with explicit cost-model (tokens/sec * cost_per_token + expected latency penalty) — need to quantify cost signals with real infra costs.
4) Investigate pre-emptible kernel eviction vs cooperative migration: can we migrate KV slices to DRAM when a kernel needs to grow workspace?
5) Add functional tests for precision-sensitive failure modes (FP16 drift on long prefixes).

Quick decision log (actual decisions we made during the lab):
- Keep TRT enabled in Dedicated pools with pre-warm policy (min-resident-workers = 2).
- For hosted API, default to Triton dynamic but auto-upgrade route to TRT when usage > X tokens/min for 3 consecutive minutes.
- Enable KV shadowing behind a feature flag and cap per-session shadow size to 8MB by default.

Next steps (concrete):
- Samir: build 'thin-loader' POC (ENG-2202) — estimate 2 weeks.
- Evan: add mem-spike profiler hooks and short window traces to the harness — 1 week.
- Clara: add FP16 long-prefix evaluation to the eval suite + generate failing prompt set.
- Aarti: consolidate heuristic into a proto-design doc for scheduling decisions and cost-model inputs.

References and links (internal):
- github PR: feature/lab-trt-fallback (#482)
- Jira: ENG-2148 (KV shadowing)
- Confluence: Serving Runtime — Kernel Integration Lab Notes
- Slack thread: #eng-runtime: "trt warmup patterns" (Dec 3 thread)

Appendix: raw numbers (selected run):
- Short-chat single request (TRT FP16): p50 42ms, p95 110ms, cold-start first request 520ms, mean GPU mem 13.8GB.
- Short-chat single request (Triton dyn): p50 61ms, p95 130ms, cold-start 120ms, mean GPU mem 11.2GB.
- Long-chat streaming (with KV shadow) TRT->Triton fallback: resume penalty median 58ms, 95th 170ms.
- Bursty-batch 100 conc short requests: with hysteresis on scheduler p95 improved from 480ms -> 390ms; kernel switch events reduced 78%.

Notes: these are measured on an rtx-a6000-like instance in our staging lab; numbers will differ on V100/4xA100 setups. Quality metrics are preliminary and should be validated by the eval team before any rollout.

If you pick this up: please add observations directly inline and mark experiments completed with dates (we should aim to keep this journal updated as we run more controlled tests).
